definition: A classification of computer organisations by their instruction and data streams: SISD, SIMD, MISD and MIMD. Flynn’s 1972 paper develops this stream-level classification; a machine can combine classes at different levels.
example: A multicore CPU is MIMD across its cores, while each core's AVX instructions are SIMD.

definition: The sequence of instructions one processor (or core) fetches and executes. Flynn's taxonomy counts how many independent instruction streams a machine runs at once.
example: Three cores running a browser, a compiler and a music player are three instruction streams.

definition: In Flynn's taxonomy, the flow of data elements an instruction stream operates on. One instruction applied to eight array elements at once acts on eight data streams.

Single instruction, single data: Flynn's class for a processor that applies one instruction to one data element at a time. It is the mental model of a simple scalar CPU, even though real cores overlap work internally.

Multiple instruction, single data: Flynn’s class with multiple instruction streams acting on one data stream. A proposed example needs an explicit account of those streams; redundant execution is not automatically MISD.

Multiple instruction, multiple data: independent instruction streams operate on multiple data streams. Multicore CPUs and clusters can execute this way, including when participants share data or run the same program.
example: An 8-core laptop running eight different programs at once is MIMD.

definition: Single program, multiple data: a programming style in which participants run the same program on different data and may take different branches. It can run on MIMD hardware or SIMT GPUs; MPI also permits other styles.

Single instruction, multiple threads: NVIDIA's name for its GPU execution model. You write scalar code for one thread; the hardware groups threads into 32-thread warps and issues each instruction to the warp's active threads.

Gustafson's measure of speedup when the problem grows with the machine: how long one processor would take for the larger job, divided by the parallel run time. With a fixed serial fraction it grows linearly with the processor count.
example: With 10% serial time on 64 processors, scaled speedup is 0.1 + 0.9 × 64 = 57.7×.

definition: Speedup divided by the number of processors, a dimensionless ratio often written as a percentage. Linear speedup gives 100%; superlinear measured speedup can exceed 100%, so it is not a literal measure of each core’s busy time.
example: A 6× speedup on 8 cores is 6 / 8 = 75% efficient.

definition: Speedup equal to processor count for the stated baseline and workload, giving parallel efficiency of 100%. This is an ideal comparison; different work or improved cache residency can produce other scaling curves.

A measured speedup greater than processor count relative to a stated one-processor baseline. Better cache residency is one possible explanation; changed algorithmic work and baseline differences must also be checked.
example: A measured 9.2-fold gain on eight cores is superlinear relative to that baseline, prompting a check of work, cache behaviour and measurement conditions.

definition: In Amdahl's law, the share of a program's one-processor run time that can be divided among processors, written p and between 0 and 1.
example: A program that spends 90 s of a 100 s run in a loop that splits perfectly has a parallel fraction of 0.9.

definition: The fraction of a stated runtime that does not shrink by distributing useful work. Amdahl measures it on the one-processor fixed-job run; Gustafson measures it on the parallel scaled-job run. Input and merge work are serial only when the implementation makes them so.
example: With fixed work and unchanged serial duration, a five-percent serial fraction gives Amdahl’s ideal twenty-fold speedup limit.

definition: Running a fixed-size problem on more processors to make it finish sooner. Amdahl's law describes its limit.
example: Rendering one frame on 8 cores instead of 1 is strong scaling.

definition: Growing the problem in step with the number of processors, keeping work per processor roughly constant, and checking that run time stays flat. Gustafson's scaled speedup is related to it.
example: Doubling both the simulation grid and the node count, and seeing the same run time, is good weak scaling.

definition: The experimentally determined serial fraction obtained by solving Amdahl’s model for a measured speedup and processor count. A rise can indicate changing overhead or execution conditions; a negative value can arise from superlinear speedup and is not a literal serial-code fraction.
example: A 6× speedup on 8 cores gives a Karp–Flatt value of about 0.048.

definition: Uneven division of work among processors, so some finish early and wait while the slowest one sets the finish time. It lowers speedup even when all the work is parallel.
Time parallel workers spend coordinating instead of computing: waiting at locks and barriers or exchanging messages. It often grows with the number of workers.
A synchronisation point that every participating thread must reach before any may continue. CUDA's __syncthreads() is a barrier for one thread block.
Messages and data transfers used to maintain cache coherence, such as ownership requests and invalidations. Sharing patterns, protocol and hardware determine their bandwidth and time costs.
Message Passing Interface: a standard library interface for programs that run as many processes, often on many machines, and exchange data by sending messages. It is the workhorse of HPC.
A United States national research laboratory where John Gustafson and colleagues ran the 1,024-processor experiments behind Gustafson's law in 1988.

A processor register holding multiple elements for vector instructions. Element width and the effective register width determine lane count; x86 fixed widths and Arm’s scalable-vector state have different contracts.
example: A 256-bit AVX register holds eight 32-bit floats.

definition: One element position in a SIMD operation. The logical lane count follows register width divided by element width; it does not by itself specify physical execution units, instruction latency or throughput.
example: 256 bits / 32 bits = 8 float32 lanes.

definition: XMM, YMM and ZMM name 128-bit, 256-bit and 512-bit x86 vector-register views on targets supporting the corresponding extensions. Where the views exist for the same register number, XMM is the low 128 bits of YMM and YMM is the low 256 bits of ZMM. A YMM register itself is 256 bits, not 128 or 512 bits.
Arm's 128-bit SIMD instruction set, officially called Advanced SIMD, available on most Arm application processors. Types such as float32x4_t hold four float lanes.

Arm’s Scalable Vector Extension. Current ordinary non-streaming SVE defines effective lengths of 128, 256, 512, 1024 or 2048 bits within the implementation and execution environment’s supported limits. Correct vector-length-agnostic code adapts to the effective length; SVE2 adds operations.

Fused multiply-add: one instruction that computes a × b + c with a single rounding at the end. Peak FLOP figures count it as two operations, and the single rounding can change results compared with a separate multiply and add.
example: Two 8-lane FMA units give 2 × 8 × 2 = 32 FLOPs per cycle.

definition: Floating-point operation: one arithmetic operation, such as an add or multiply, on floating-point numbers. FLOP counts measure work; FLOP/s measure speed.
example: A dot product of two 1,000-element vectors is about 2,000 FLOPs.

definition: Billions (10^9) of floating-point operations per second, a common unit of arithmetic throughput.
example: A core doing 32 FLOPs per cycle at 3 GHz peaks at 96 GFLOP/s.

definition: Trillions (10^12) of floating-point operations per second, 1,000 GFLOP/s. GPU and accelerator peaks are usually quoted in it.

A register whose mask or predicate bits select participating vector elements. AVX-512 has eight opmask registers; ordinary EVEX writemasking uses k1–k7 because a zero mask field means no writemask. SVE has its own predicate-register rules.
Functions a C or C++ compiler provides that map almost one-to-one onto particular machine instructions, such as _mm256_add_ps for AVX vaddps. They give hand control of SIMD without writing assembly.
The short scalar loop after a vectorised loop that handles the elements left over when the count is not a multiple of the lane count.
example: For 1,003 floats in 8-lane vectors, the tail loop handles the last 3.

definition: A load whose address lacks the instruction’s natural alignment. AVX loadu intrinsics accept unaligned addresses, but every accessed byte must still be valid; costs depend on the target and boundaries crossed.

A C keyword establishing an access-based pointer contract for a block execution. If an object is modified through a restricted pointer, relevant accesses must use that pointer’s permitted derivations; two read-only inputs may still alias. Violating the contract can give undefined behaviour.
example: void add(float *restrict a, ...)

definition: A dependency in which one loop iteration needs a result from an earlier iteration, so the iterations cannot run independently in separate lanes.
example: a[i] = a[i - 1] * 0.5f + b[i] has a loop-carried dependency on a[i - 1].

definition: Combining many values into one, such as a sum or maximum. A vector implementation may use partial results and reassociation, but some targets support ordered reductions; legality and numerical behaviour depend on the operation and contract.

Changing how operations are grouped. Mathematical integer addition and multiplication are associative; fixed-width unsigned addition wraps modulo its width, while signed C overflow is undefined. Floating-point regrouping can change rounding, overflow and cancellation results.
example: In float32, first cancelling equal large opposite values and then adding one can differ from first adding one to one of the large values.

definition: Compiler options (such as GCC and Clang -ffast-math) that relax strict IEEE floating-point rules: allowing reassociation, ignoring NaN and infinity cases, and more. They can speed code up and also change or break numerical results.

Replacing control-flow selection with data selection, predication or masked work. The transformation must preserve required side effects and avoid introducing invalid accesses or exceptions; it cannot always evaluate both paths unconditionally.
example: b[i] > 0 ? b[i] : 0 becomes a compare and a per-lane select.

definition: A vector load taking elements from indexed addresses rather than one contiguous range. Availability and relative cost depend on the target, addresses, cache state and element type.
In NumPy, an array's element data type, such as float32 or int8. It sets how many bytes each element takes and which compiled (and possibly SIMD) loop handles an operation.
Shipping several compiled versions of a hot function (for example baseline SSE2 and AVX2) and choosing one at run time after checking which features the CPU and operating system support.

The x86 instruction that reports a processor's identity and supported features, such as whether AVX2 exists. Feature bits alone do not show that the operating system has enabled the matching register state.
An x86 CPUID feature flag meaning the operating system has enabled the XSAVE mechanism for saving extended register state. Code must check it, then XGETBV, before using AVX.

The x86 instruction that reads an extended-control register such as XCR0. XCR0 reports enabled extended processor state; an AVX dispatcher checks the relevant CPU and operating-system support rather than assuming one feature bit is sufficient.
The Unix signal a program receives when the CPU meets an instruction it does not implement or that is not allowed. Running AVX2 code on a CPU without AVX2 raises it.

GCC and Clang target options that permit particular instruction sets or processor features. A -march CPU target can enable several extensions, while -mavx2 enables AVX2; -march=native targets the build machine and can make a binary incompatible with older deployment CPUs.
The order in which one thread's instructions appear in its program. Memory models describe which program-order pairs other threads may observe in a different order.
One way of merging several threads' operations into a single sequence that keeps each thread's own order. Sequential consistency allows any interleaving and nothing else.
A tiny multi-threaded program, with a question about which final values are possible, used to pin down what a memory model allows.
example: The store-buffering test asks whether both threads can read 0.

definition: The litmus test in which each of two threads stores to one variable, then loads the other. Sequential consistency forbids both loads returning 0; x86-TSO and Arm allow it because stores can wait in a store buffer.
First in, first out: items leave a queue in the order they entered. An x86 store buffer drains in FIFO order, so stores become visible in program order.

An instruction stream the processor tracks with its own registers and program counter. A core with simultaneous multithreading runs two or more hardware threads, each with its own store buffer in the x86-TSO model.

A memory model that lets loads and stores to different addresses become visible out of program order unless the program adds barriers, dependencies or ordered instructions. Arm and POWER are weakly ordered.
Arm's memory type for ordinary RAM, where the processor may cache, merge and reorder accesses. Device memory, used for hardware registers, has stricter rules.

A memory/cache policy under which a modified cached line may remain dirty before a later writeback. Coherence can make writes observable to other cores before DRAM is updated; eviction is not the only possible cause of writeback.
Memory-mapped input/output: device registers that appear at memory addresses, so ordinary loads and stores control hardware. Such accesses have their own ordering rules outside the x86-TSO model.

An ordering operation with a specified scope and access contract. Hardware barriers constrain the machine model; compiler barriers constrain compiler transformations. A hardware instruction alone does not repair a C/C++ data race on ordinary objects.

An x86 instruction that orders relevant earlier loads and stores before later loads and stores. Within the stated ordinary write-back TSO model, it establishes the store-before-load order needed to exclude the store-buffering both-zero outcome when correctly placed.
An x86 store fence that orders earlier stores before later stores. Ordinary x86 stores are already ordered, so it matters mainly for non-temporal stores.
The x86 exchange instruction. With a memory operand it is implicitly locked, so it is atomic and a full barrier; compilers use it for sequentially consistent stores.

Arm’s Data Memory Barrier instruction. With the required shareability scope, DMB ISH orders relevant earlier and later data accesses; ISHST orders stores before stores, while ISHLD orders earlier loads before later loads and stores. It is not a general cache flush.

An Arm shareability domain defined by the system, used to scope operations such as DMB ISH. Correct software must use the domain covering the observers that need ordering rather than assume it is every processor everywhere.

An AArch64 load-acquire instruction with the architecture’s RCsc acquire ordering. It constrains later relevant accesses; language-level synchronisation still requires a valid protocol and an appropriate read-from relation.

An AArch64 store-release instruction that orders relevant earlier accesses before its store. It can implement language release stores, but neither its existence nor a compiler mapping makes an arbitrary publication protocol correct.

An AArch64 RCpc load-acquire instruction provided by FEAT_LRCPC. It has weaker ordering than LDAR in some patterns, including interaction with an earlier STLR; mapping choices and performance depend on the target and compiler.
Arm's Large System Extensions (Armv8.1): single atomic read-modify-write instructions such as LDADDAL, replacing loops of exclusive loads and stores.

An atomic-update pattern using exclusive load/store instructions and retrying when the conditional store fails. Failure can occur for reasons other than another write, including loss of the exclusive reservation; ordering depends on the selected instructions and barriers.

An ordering contract commonly used for a load. When it reads the appropriate value from a release operation, the language synchronisation relation makes relevant earlier writes happen before later reads; acquire alone does not publish unrelated data.

An ordering contract commonly used for a store. An acquire operation that reads the appropriate released value can synchronise with it, ordering the releasing thread’s earlier work before the acquiring thread’s later work.

C/C++ sequentially consistent atomic ordering, the default for ordinary atomic APIs. Applicable operations have acquire/release effects and participate in a single order satisfying the standard’s constraints; mixing weaker operations does not make every action globally sequentially consistent.

C/C++ atomic ordering that supplies atomicity and per-object modification-order constraints without publishing unrelated data. A relaxed read-modify-write can safely update an independent statistic; a separate load followed by a store is not an atomic increment.

A machine-level test where one thread writes data then a flag and another reads the flag then data. With the lesson’s ordinary aligned coherent memory assumptions, x86-TSO forbids seeing the new flag with old data; Arm needs suitable ordering. Unsynchronised C/C++ ordinary objects would instead cause a data race.

A memory-model constraint on the propagation order in which observers see writes. Other-multi-copy atomicity permits an issuing thread to read its own buffered write early while constraining propagation to other observers; it is not a claim of zero physical propagation time.

Independent Reads of Independent Writes: two writers update different words and two readers read them in opposite orders. With each reader’s loads suitably ordered, opposite observations of write order are forbidden by the stated multicopy-atomic hardware model; unordered readers or language acquire mappings require separate analysis.

The sequential-consistency guarantee for a data-race-free program using mutexes and seq_cst atomic operations without weaker synchronisation operations. Being data-race-free alone does not make a program using weaker atomics sequentially consistent.

A C/C++ synchronisation relation. For the atomic publication pattern here, a release operation synchronises with an acquire operation that reads from its release sequence, making relevant earlier work happen before the acquiring thread’s later work. Other synchronisation operations have their own rules.
An atomic operation that reads a value, changes it and writes it back as one indivisible step, such as fetch_add. Separate load and store can lose updates when two threads interleave.
The 2011 revisions of the C and C++ standards, the first to define a memory model for threads, with atomics and memory orderings.

In C/C++, volatile accesses obey implementation-specific observable-access rules, often used with device registers. The qualifier does not provide inter-thread atomicity or synchronisation. Java volatile has a different language contract and should be consulted separately.
A tool built into Clang and GCC that instruments a program to detect data races while it runs.
example: Compile with -fsanitize=thread.

definition: A two-participant mutual-exclusion algorithm using flags and a turn variable. The standard algorithm is correct under sequential consistency; ordinary x86-TSO assembly needs suitable store-before-load ordering, such as correctly placed full fences. A C/C++ implementation must additionally obey language atomicity and ordering rules.

Apple’s translation environment for running supported x86-64 applications on Apple silicon. Instruction support and translation behaviour depend on the macOS version; this definition makes no claim about an undocumented hardware mode or a universal performance benefit.
A later load completing before an earlier store to a different address becomes visible. It is the one reordering x86-TSO permits, caused by the store buffer.
NVIDIA's platform and C++ extensions for running general-purpose programs on its GPUs: you write kernels that run as many threads, launched as a grid of thread blocks.

An NVIDIA GPU execution block containing resources such as warp schedulers, registers, shared memory and execution units. Ordinary thread blocks reside on one SM; resource sizes, block limits and SM counts vary by target.

NVIDIA’s name for certain scalar arithmetic execution resources within an SM. The supported operations and throughput depend on the GPU; such a resource is not equivalent to a general CPU core with its own independent instruction stream.

A function that performs one piece of data-parallel or numeric work, such as an array add or a matrix multiply. On a GPU it describes what one thread does and is launched over many threads; in performance work, 'kernel' means any such hot loop. Not the operating-system kernel.
example: saxpy<<<blocks, 256>>>(n, 2.0f, dx, dy) launches a GPU kernel.

definition: The thread blocks created by one CUDA kernel launch. Ordinary blocks must be independently schedulable; cooperative and cluster features provide additional explicit synchronisation contracts on supported targets.
A group of up to 1,024 CUDA threads that runs on a single SM, can share that SM's shared memory and can synchronise with __syncthreads(). Its threads are split into warps of 32.
example: A block of 256 threads is 8 warps.

definition: One logical CUDA kernel thread with its own execution state and block/thread indices. A launch may expose thousands of threads; hardware groups consecutive linear block-thread indices into warps and issues instructions to active participants subject to resource limits.

A group of 32 consecutive linear thread indices within a CUDA block. Instructions issue to active participants; this logical grouping does not guarantee one-cycle execution or implicit lockstep synchronisation.
example: Threads 0–31 of a block form warp 0, threads 32–63 warp 1.

definition: A CUDA built-in giving a thread's index within its block (with x, y and z parts).
A CUDA built-in giving the index of the current block within the grid.
A CUDA built-in giving the number of threads per block in each dimension.
The position of a CUDA thread across the whole grid, usually blockIdx.x × blockDim.x + threadIdx.x, used to pick which array element the thread handles.
example: Thread 10 of block 3 with 256-thread blocks has global index 778.

definition: Single-precision a times x plus y: y[i] = a × x[i] + y[i] over arrays. A standard small benchmark and teaching kernel; DAXPY is the double-precision version.

Double-precision scaled-vector addition: multiply each element of an input by a scalar and add it to the corresponding output element. Under the lesson’s streaming model, reading two 8-byte values and eventually writing one gives two FLOPs per 24 bytes; caching and other traffic models can differ.
CUDA’s block-wide barrier and memory-ordering primitive. Participation must satisfy the documented control-flow rules; calling it on only an arbitrary subset of active block threads can be invalid.

CUDA’s barrier and memory-ordering primitive for participating warp threads named by a mask. Every required non-exited participant must execute the matching operation; warp membership alone is not a synchronisation contract.

Programmer-managed memory associated with a CUDA SM and allocated to resident blocks. Ordinary block shared memory is accessible within its block; supported cluster facilities extend access under their own synchronisation and lifetime rules. Capacity and access costs vary by target.

CUDA cluster functionality on supported devices that lets a block address shared memory belonging to other blocks in its thread-block cluster. Correct cluster synchronisation and storage lifetimes are required.

A supported CUDA grouping of thread blocks guaranteed to be co-scheduled within one GPU Processing Cluster (GPC). It enables explicit cluster synchronisation and distributed shared-memory access under documented participation and lifetime rules; physical adjacency of individual SMs is not the contract.

CUDA memory addressable across the grid subject to allocation, lifetime and memory-ordering rules. It is not limited to a single physical DRAM technology: supported mapped or managed allocations can have different locations and access costs.

When active threads of a warp choose different control-flow paths. A simplified masked-path model executes the paths separately; actual scheduling, predication and elapsed cost depend on the code and target, so path times do not universally add exactly.
example: In a stated no-overlap masked-path model, paths costing 100 and 60 cycles take about 160 cycles together; actual device timing requires measurement.

definition: NVIDIA's model since Volta (2017) in which each thread of a warp has its own program counter, so threads may run apart. Code must not assume the warp moves in lockstep.

An NVIDIA GPU architecture introducing independent thread scheduling and tensor-core operations. Its scheduling contract means software must use documented synchronisation instead of assuming implicit warp lockstep.
Several threads executing the same instruction at the same moment. CUDA does not guarantee it for a warp, so it cannot be used for synchronisation.
Keeping execution units busy during a slow operation by switching to other ready work. GPUs hide memory latency by keeping many warps resident and issuing from whichever is ready.

A warp whose execution state occupies resources on an SM. A scheduler can select ready resident work without an operating-system context switch; residency does not guarantee readiness or a free scheduling operation.

Resident warps divided by the selected SM’s maximum resident warps. Registers, block shared memory and whole-block limits constrain it. More occupancy can expose useful independent work but does not guarantee better performance.
example: A 64-warp SM holding 16 warps is at 25% occupancy.

definition: Combining participating GPU threads’ memory accesses into memory transactions or requested sectors according to the target’s rules. In the stated 32-byte-sector model, 32 aligned consecutive 4-byte loads touch four sectors; misalignment and other patterns can differ.

A 32-byte requested memory unit in the NVIDIA access model used in these lessons. Sector counts describe the requested access footprint; cache hits and lower-level transfer rules mean they are not automatically counts of DRAM transfers.

One independently addressed subdivision of CUDA shared memory. In the lesson’s 32-bank, 4-byte-word model, different words in one bank can require multiple service passes; same-word reads can broadcast. Padding can remove a particular access conflict.
example: Reading a column of float tile[32][32] puts all 32 threads in one bank: a 32-way conflict.

definition: An NVIDIA execution resource for supported matrix operations. Operand shapes, numerical formats, accumulation rules and throughput depend on the GPU and instruction; some targets support FP64 matrix operations as well as reduced-precision modes.

PCI Express, an interconnect used to attach devices including many discrete GPUs. Effective transfer bandwidth depends on generation, lane count, direction and system configuration; the lesson’s 25 GB/s is an explicit example assumption.
example: 4 GB at 25 GB/s takes 0.16 s.

definition: A CUDA facility representing a dependency graph of operations such as kernel launches and copies for repeated execution. It can reduce submission overhead for appropriate workloads; capture, update and execution rules depend on the API and target.

Combining operations into a kernel or loop to avoid materialising some intermediates and possibly reduce launches. Savings depend on data types, traffic and reuse; changed register pressure and numerical contraction must also be checked.
example: For separate float32 passes with no cache reuse or write allocation, eliminating one intermediate store and later load saves eight bytes per element; other traffic models differ.

definition: Memory of the host system, as distinguished from an accelerator’s own memory. GPU access may use explicit copies, mapped memory, managed memory or coherent system facilities depending on the platform.

CUDA managed-memory facilities providing allocations accessible to host and device. Migration, remote access, coherence and performance depend on the system and API contract; sharing a pointer does not promise identical access costs everywhere.
NVIDIA’s A100 data-centre GPU family, based on the Ampere architecture. Resource counts, memory configurations and peak rates must be taken from the selected product specification.
32-bit IEEE 754 floating point (binary32): 1 sign, 8 exponent and 23 fraction bits, about 7 decimal digits of precision.

IEEE 754 binary64 floating point: one sign bit, eleven exponent bits and 52 stored fraction bits, giving about sixteen decimal digits of precision. C double commonly uses binary64 on the targets discussed; C itself does not mandate that exact representation.
An 8-bit integer type, range −128 to 127 when signed. Used for quantised neural-network inference, as in TPU v1.
Multiply-accumulate: multiply two numbers and add the product to a running total (acc ← acc + a × b). The basic step of dot products and matrix multiplies; peak figures count it as two operations.
The TPU's main compute block: a large grid of MAC cells arranged as a systolic array that multiplies matrices.

An array of processing elements with a regular, rhythmic local dataflow, often forwarding operands or partial results between neighbours. A matrix-multiply design can reuse operands across many multiply-accumulate operations; the precise operation, dataflow and busy cycles depend on the design.

A computing cell in a parallel array. In this module’s matrix-array model, each cell multiplies a pair of operands, accumulates a result and participates in the stated neighbour dataflow; other arrays may use different operations.
A systolic-array schedule in which each PE keeps one output element and accumulates it while inputs flow past.
A systolic-array schedule in which neural-network weights are preloaded into the PEs and stay put, while activations flow across and partial sums flow down. TPU v1 used it.
Running an already-trained neural network to make predictions, as opposed to training it. It can use lower precision such as int8.

Adjusting a machine-learning model’s parameters from data. Numerical formats and accumulation requirements depend on the algorithm and implementation; bfloat16, float32 and other formats may be combined.

A learned parameter used in a neural network’s computation. Keeping weights available for several examples can improve reuse; actual physical reads depend on tiling, caches, batch size and the execution schedule.
A neural-network layer in which every output is a weighted sum of every input: a matrix-vector (or, for a batch, matrix-matrix) multiply.

The number of inputs grouped for one execution. A larger batch can increase reuse or utilisation in some workloads; requests may wait for batch formation, so throughput and latency need separate measurement.
Accelerated Linear Algebra: Google's compiler that turns machine-learning computations (from JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch) into code for TPUs, GPUs and CPUs.
Representing values with fewer bits, such as int8 instead of float32, to cut memory and arithmetic cost at some loss of accuracy.
Using different floating-point formats in one computation, for example bfloat16 multiplies with float32 accumulation.
Tera-operations per second: one trillion operations each second. State the operation type and counting convention; accelerator figures commonly count a multiply and an add as two operations.

An FPGA hard arithmetic block supporting operations such as multiplication and accumulation, with device-specific modes. It can implement those functions without constructing the entire datapath from LUTs; area and timing comparisons depend on the design.
Dedicated on-chip memory blocks in an FPGA, available as resources for a hardware design. Their sizes, port modes and supported configurations depend on the device.
Tools that turn a restricted C, C++ or similar program into a hardware design for an FPGA or ASIC.

The process of meeting a hardware design’s timing constraints, including setup and hold requirements and specified clock relationships. Logic delay, routing and implementation choices matter; not every path is constrained by one universal clock period.
In a hardware pipeline, the number of clock cycles between accepting successive inputs. An interval of 1 means one new input every cycle.
A processor built from an FPGA's configurable logic rather than fixed silicon, for example AMD's MicroBlaze.
Double Data Rate 3 synchronous DRAM, a generation of external memory technology. The first TPU described in the 2017 paper used 8 GiB of DDR3 weight memory at about 34 GB/s.

High Bandwidth Memory: stacked DRAM connected through a wide interface, used by supported GPUs and TPU generations. The selected product determines memory capacity, placement and achievable bandwidth.
An NVIDIA data-centre GPU family used for the GPU comparison in the 2017 first-TPU paper. The paper’s compared system and workload are required context for its performance ratios.
An Intel CPU microarchitecture supporting AVX2 and FMA. Haswell-based CPUs were the CPU comparison in the 2017 first-TPU paper; actual throughput depends on the selected processor and workload.
The start and end of a pipelined or systolic computation when only some units have work, which lowers average utilisation for short jobs.

The fraction of a stated hardware resource capacity used for the chosen work. State the denominator: useful processing-element cycles, active lane capacity and requested memory-sector bytes are different measurements and must not be treated as interchangeable.

Sending part of a computation from a host processor to an accelerator. To reduce elapsed time, the saved computation must outweigh added transfers, setup and synchronisation after accounting for any valid overlap; energy and throughput objectives need their own comparisons.
Keeping data in an accelerator's memory across many operations so it is not copied back and forth each time.

A performance model by Williams, Waterman and Patterson (2009): a kernel's attainable FLOP rate is the lower of the machine's peak compute and its memory bandwidth times the kernel's arithmetic intensity. On log–log axes it looks like a roof.
example: At 0.5 FLOP/byte and 200 GB/s, a kernel can reach at most 100 GFLOP/s.

definition: Arithmetic operations performed per byte transferred at a stated memory level using a stated traffic convention. Combined with consistent bandwidth and compute ceilings, it bounds performance; intensity alone does not prove the observed bottleneck.
example: Vector add on doubles: 1 FLOP per 32 bytes, about 0.03 FLOP/byte.

definition: The arithmetic intensity where a specified bandwidth ceiling meets a specified compute ceiling in a roofline model. To the left, bandwidth is the lower model ceiling; actual performance may be limited by other resources.
example: 1,000 GFLOP/s / 100 GB/s = 10 FLOP/byte.

definition: One of the limiting lines on a roofline plot: the flat compute roof, the sloped bandwidth roof, or lower ceilings such as peak without SIMD or bandwidth from one core.
The highest arithmetic rate a processor could reach if every unit did useful work every cycle: cores × clock rate × FLOPs per core per cycle. Real code usually reaches a fraction of it.
John McCalpin's standard benchmark of sustainable memory bandwidth, using simple vector kernels such as copy and triad. It counts useful array bytes, not write-allocate traffic.
Intel's performance analysis tool, which can measure FLOPs and memory traffic and draw roofline charts.
NVIDIA's profiler for GPU kernels, reporting detailed counters and roofline charts.
Performance monitoring unit: the hardware in a processor that counts events such as cycles, instructions retired, cache misses and branch misses. Tools such as perf read it.
The Linux perf commands that sample where a program spends its events (perf record) and summarise the samples by function (perf report).
example: perf record -g ./app; perf report

definition: A profiler that records execution locations or stacks at selected time intervals or event counts. Samples estimate the distribution of the chosen event; overhead, precision, blocked-time coverage and bias depend on the method and settings.
The gap between the instruction that caused a sampled event and the instruction the profiler records, so samples can land a few instructions late.
Brendan Gregg's visualisation of sampled call stacks: each box is a function, its width is the share of samples that include it, and callers sit below callees. Left-to-right order is not time.

A model-specific opportunity to allocate or account for a micro-operation in Intel top-down analysis. Available slots per cycle depend on the processor and metric; a slot share is not directly an elapsed-time share.
Top-down category for slots lost because the front end (fetch and decode) did not deliver micro-operations in time.

Intel top-down category attributing slots to backend resource pressure, such as execution resources or the memory subsystem. It is refined into core-bound and memory-bound categories under processor-specific metrics; the percentage is not directly an elapsed-time fraction.

Intel top-down category for slots lost to incorrect speculation, including issued micro-operations that do not retire and slots blocked during recovery. Branch mispredictions and machine clears can contribute; the exact metric is processor-specific.
Top-down category for slots used by micro-operations that completed and were kept.
The extra cost of the first runs of a benchmark: page faults, cold caches, lazy loading and JIT compilation. Exclude it only when steady state is what you want to measure.
A processor lowering its clock to stay within temperature or power limits, which can make later benchmark runs slower than early ones.
A compiler optimisation that removes computations whose results are never used. It can delete a benchmark's work and report impossibly fast times.
example: 0.3 ns per call is about one cycle at 3 GHz: suspect deleted work.

definition: A clock that does not go backwards during its documented operation, suitable for interval measurement. Adjustment rate and whether suspension is included depend on the clock; monotonic does not necessarily mean immune to rate corrections.
Python's high-resolution monotonic timer for measuring short intervals.
Python's standard module for timing small snippets by running them many times; it disables garbage collection by default.
A benchmark that times one small piece of code in isolation. Easy to get wrong because of warm-up, dead-code elimination and frequency changes.
An instruction the core has finished and committed, as opposed to work done speculatively and discarded. IPC counts retired instructions.
A CPython 3.12+ option on supported Linux builds that lets perf show Python function names in its profiles.
Hardware entries that track outstanding cache misses, limiting how many memory requests one core can have in flight at once.
The x86 instruction that adds packed single-precision floats lane by lane: four with 128-bit SSE (addps), eight with 256-bit AVX ymm registers, sixteen with AVX-512.
example: vaddps ymm0, ymm1, ymm2 adds eight float pairs.

definition: A group of separate computers connected by a network and used together as one parallel machine; a classic MIMD system.
Compiler output saying which loops were vectorised and why others were not, e.g. GCC -fopt-info-vec-missed or Clang -Rpass-missed=loop-vectorize.
A database that stores each column's values together rather than each row's, a structure-of-arrays layout that suits scans and SIMD.

The submission and scheduling costs associated with starting device work. Their size depends on the platform, API and workload; include them in the relevant end-to-end measurement rather than assuming a universal fixed duration.

Executing an operation only for selected participating lanes or threads. Inactive-result behaviour depends on the instruction: some preserve prior values, others use zeroing or other defined behaviour.

SM hardware that selects ready warp instructions for issue subject to dependencies and execution resources. Scheduler count and issue behaviour are target-specific; a ready warp is not a guarantee of one issued instruction on every cycle.
The network of wires and configurable switches in an FPGA that connects logic blocks as the bitstream specifies.
10^-12 joules, a unit used for the energy of single arithmetic operations and memory accesses.
The SI unit of energy; one watt for one second. Accelerator efficiency is often operations per joule.
Deferring code or data loading until it is first needed. This can add a first-use cost; whether that cost belongs in a benchmark depends on the measured objective.
Short for floating point, as in FP32 or FP reduction semantics.

A cache that can continue serving some requests while misses are outstanding. Finite tracking resources, dependencies and conflicts constrain this ability; it does not promise every later load completes first.
The company that designs NVIDIA GPUs and the CUDA platform discussed in this module.
Terabytes per second: 10^12 bytes per second, 1,000 GB/s. Modern GPU memory bandwidth is quoted in it.

A processor built to execute a broad set of programs through a programmable instruction set. Implementations may overlap, reorder and vectorise work internally; generality also requires control and data movement resources.

A chain of hardware stages that can process different inputs concurrently. The initiation interval controls acceptance rate and the stage timing contributes latency; stalls, backpressure and memory access can alter the achieved behaviour.
example: Under explicit no-stall assumptions, a 300 MHz pipeline accepting one complete packet per cycle sustains 300 million packets per second; packet latency still depends on the pipeline.

definition: A build configured to support debugging, for example through symbols or reduced optimisation. Debug symbols alone do not require optimisation to be disabled; performance comparisons should use the intended production configuration.
One billion floating-point operations, a count of arithmetic work. GFLOP/s is the corresponding rate per second; the operation and FMA counting convention must be stated.
One trillion floating-point operations, a count of arithmetic work. TFLOP/s counts that amount of work per second; it is a rate and depends on the stated numerical operation.
NVIDIA’s Hopper-generation data-centre GPU family. Memory configurations, resource counts and operation throughput depend on the selected product; H100 is not an alias for A100.

A memory model without the stated multicopy-atomic propagation constraint. Under suitable weaker-model rules, different observers can see independent writes in inconsistent orders even when each reader’s own loads are ordered. The exact allowed outcomes depend on the complete architecture and barrier model.
One billion counted operations per second. State which operations and numerical precision are being counted; TOPS is one thousand GOPS.

Changing a processor’s operating clock frequency under a hardware or software policy. Power limits, temperature and workload can affect the selected clock; it is one reason benchmark conditions and sustained rates matter.

Moving values between storage locations or processing resources, such as reading memory into a processor or copying host data to a device. Its traffic, latency and energy costs must be included in the chosen performance model; a particular copy API is not required for every movement.

Useful bytes requested by participating threads divided by the bytes covered by the requested GPU memory sectors. This is a byte-footprint ratio, distinct from the fraction of time an execution unit is busy; caches can make actual DRAM traffic different.

The Intel top-down backend subcategory for execution-core resource pressure rather than the memory-bound subcategory. The exact metrics depend on the processor; its slot share is not directly elapsed time.

Slots attributed to memory-related backend pressure in the selected Intel top-down metrics. This can include several memory-system constraints and is not automatically a fraction of elapsed time spent waiting for loads.

A GCC option allowing floating-point reassociation that can change rounding, signed-zero, NaN and overflow behaviour. GCC requires compatible -fno-signed-zeros and -fno-trapping-math settings; it is one relaxation and is not identical to the entire -ffast-math bundle.
